set.explanation: Troponin confirms myocardial necrosis and adds prognosis, but with ST elevation primary PCI is arranged on the ECG alone. Stress tests and CT angiography are for stable pain.
Every ACS patient gets aspirin (300 mg load, then 75 mg daily) plus a P2Y12 inhibitor. Amlodipine has no prognostic benefit and HbA1c 6.3% needs no extra drug.
Most MI deaths are early (often pre-hospital) from ventricular fibrillation; hence monitoring and rapid defibrillation. Cardiogenic shock dominates later in-hospital deaths.
Sharp positional pain with low-grade fever 1–3 days after a transmural MI is early post-infarct pericarditis; treat with aspirin. Dressler syndrome comes weeks later.
Prognosis after MI improves with DAPT, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker (± MRA/SGLT2i if LVEF low). Amlodipine only relieves angina or lowers BP.
Load a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel) with aspirin before primary PCI. In inferior STEMI with hypotension, beta-blockers, diltiazem and nitrates can cause shock.
Rising troponin with dynamic ST depression is NSTEMI (high risk): angiography within 24 h. Immediate (< 2 h) only if unstable; CKD needs hydration, not delay.
In dissection give an IV beta-blocker (labetalol/esmolol) first: target HR < 60/min and SBP 100–120 mmHg. Vasodilators alone cause reflex tachycardia.
Sudden pale, cold, pulseless leg with sensory loss in AF is acute arterial (embolic) occlusion. DVT gives a warm swollen leg with pulses present.
Acute limb ischaemia: IV unfractionated heparin, analgesia and urgent vascular referral for embolectomy or thrombolysis. Long-term anticoagulation follows for AF.
Thrombolysis is harmful without ST elevation and is not given > 12 h after onset even for STEMI. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, fondaparinux and beta-blocker are all appropriate.
High HDL cholesterol is protective (reverse cholesterol transport). Hypertension, diabetes and high triglycerides are risk factors for coronary disease.
Unmodifiable risk factors: age, male sex and family history of premature CAD. Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, lipids and obesity are modifiable.
Persistent ST elevation weeks after MI with a dyskinetic apical impulse is LV aneurysm; echo confirms. Risks: heart failure, VT and mural thrombus.
Claudication (chronic PAD) causes absent pulses, cool hairless skin, pallor on elevation and rubor. Paralysis belongs to acute limb ischaemia (the 6 Ps).
Stable angina: exertional tightness lasting minutes, relieved by rest or GTN within ~5 min. Rest pain > 20 min suggests ACS.
Repair an AAA at ≥ 5.5 cm, growth > 1 cm/year or if symptomatic (NICE NG156). Aneurysms of 3.0–5.4 cm are kept under ultrasound surveillance.
Unstable angina has no necrosis; ECG is normal or shows ST depression/T inversion. Persistent ST elevation means STEMI and needs immediate reperfusion.
Hypotension, raised JVP, soft heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus days after MI is tamponade from free-wall rupture. A VSD would give a loud pansystolic murmur.
After MI with LVEF ≤ 40% plus heart failure or diabetes, add an MRA (eplerenone/spironolactone) to ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker; it reduces mortality.
Anterolateral STEMI: troponin confirms necrosis among the tests listed, but reperfusion never waits for it. CTPA is for suspected PE.
STEMI < 12 h needs immediate reperfusion: primary PCI if possible within 120 min of diagnosis, otherwise fibrinolysis. Antithrombotics alone do not open the artery.
Widened mediastinum with dysphagia and breathlessness from compression in a hypertensive man suggests thoracic aortic aneurysm; confirm with CT angiography.
Untreated thoracic aneurysms dissect or rupture; risk rises steeply above ~5.5 cm (the repair threshold, lower in Marfan). Tamponade follows dissection.
Every post-MI patient should take a beta-blocker unless contraindicated; bisoprolol is preferred if EF is reduced. Furosemide is only for congestion.
Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest with a normal ECG is stable angina: GTN, antianginal drug and CT coronary angiography. Unstable angina occurs at rest.
STEMI is diagnosed on a 12-lead ECG within 10 min: ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads or new LBBB. Troponin is not needed to start reperfusion.
GRACE (age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip, arrest, ST deviation, troponin) is the recommended ACS risk score. CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED are for AF.
If primary PCI cannot be done within 120 min, give fibrinolysis (tenecteplase) within 12 h, then transfer for angiography in 2–24 h (pharmaco-invasive).
In ischaemic cardiomyopathy with angina or viable myocardium, CABG improves survival (STICH) and treats the cause. Diuretics and ICDs do not.
JVP reflects right atrial pressure; recurrent PE causes pulmonary hypertension and RV strain, raising it. Dehydration lowers the JVP.
New harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with collapse 2–5 days after anterior MI is septal rupture (VSD). Papillary rupture gives an apical MR murmur.
Troponin may be normal early: a rise above the 99th centile with dynamic change on repeat (1–3 h hs-assay) supports MI. One normal test does not exclude it.
Primary-prevention ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% ≥ 40 days after MI on optimal therapy with good life expectancy. VF within 48 h of MI is reversible; heart block needs a pacemaker.
Smoking is the lifestyle factor most strongly linked to MI (roughly doubles risk, more in the young). Stopping halves the excess risk within a few years.
Fibrinolysis benefit falls steeply with time (best within 2–3 h, small after 12 h). PCI benefit is less time-dependent; aspirin and heparin are not.
Troponin I/T are structural myofibrillar proteins, highly cardiac-specific and raised for 7–14 days. CK, CK-MB, AST and LDH are less specific enzymes.
RCA occlusion gives inferior STEMI and, as it supplies the SA and AV nodes, bradycardia and AV block. ST elevation in I, aVL, V6 is circumflex territory.
Sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension after inferior MI is posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (single blood supply) with acute MR; echo, IABP, surgery.
Sudden pulseless collapse during acute ischaemia is most often VF; immediate defibrillation restores circulation. Free-wall rupture occurs days later.
Capillary refill < 2 s shows good distal perfusion. Coldness, pallor, hair loss and absent pulses mean advanced ischaemia; ABPI < 0.9 confirms PAD.
Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): segmental arteritis in young heavy smokers with digital ischaemia and thrombophlebitis; only stopping smoking halts it.
Age is the strongest predictor of death after MI and weighs most in the GRACE score; prompt PCI after resuscitated VF carries a better outlook.
After large anterior MI, echo assesses LV function (guides ACEi, MRA, ICD) and detects apical thrombus needing anticoagulation. MRI best shows scar.
CABG gives the greatest survival benefit in left main disease and multivessel disease with LV dysfunction. One- or two-vessel disease with good LV gains symptoms only.
Late gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows scar and its transmural extent: > 50% transmural scar is unlikely to recover after revascularisation.
A peak aortic gradient of 25 mmHg is only mild AS. Recent ACS, recent stenting, severe LV dysfunction, insulin-treated diabetes and CKD raise perioperative risk.
Reaching Bruce stage 3 before ischaemia shows a high ischaemic threshold and low risk. Early ST depression or poor LV function means high risk.
Stopping smoking after MI cuts death and reinfarction by a third to a half, more than any single drug; aspirin, statin and ACE inhibitor add further benefit.
The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior ST elevation and inferior reciprocal depression (anterior STEMI). Narrow QRS with P waves excludes VT.
ST elevation in V1–V4 with reciprocal inferior depression means proximal LAD occlusion (anterior wall and septum). RCA gives inferior, circumflex lateral/posterior changes.
Pathological Q waves (> 40 ms or > ¼ of the R wave) in contiguous leads mean an old transmural infarct; echo can confirm a regional wall-motion defect.
A reversible defect in the apex, anterior wall and septum is LAD territory. Mediastinal radiotherapy accelerates coronary disease, especially of the proximal LAD.
ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and eplerenone cut early post-MI mortality; an ICD in the first 40 days does not (DINAMIT, IRIS). Reassess EF after 40 days.
Predictable exertional angina limiting ordinary activity slightly (e.g. walking uphill, stairs quickly) is CCS class II. Class III = one flight at normal pace.
The test needs ≥ 85% of age-predicted maximum HR (~145/min at 50); a peak of 130 is non-diagnostic. A BP rise to 155/95 on exercise is normal.
NSTEMI causes: non-occlusive plaque thrombus (commonest), spasm, progressive narrowing, inflammation and supply–demand mismatch. Microvascular dysfunction causes microvascular angina.
Crescendo then rest angina with new T inversion is NSTE-ACS; only troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina, so the diagnosis awaits it (treatment starts now).
A small troponin rise with fluid overload in an anuric dialysis patient is demand injury: urgent dialysis with ultrafiltration and serial troponin/ECG. Furosemide fails in anuria.
Nitrates are contraindicated within 48 h of tadalafil (24 h for sildenafil): profound hypotension. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant and beta-blocker are fine.
High-sensitivity troponin I/T is the preferred MI marker: a rise/fall with one value > 99th centile plus ischaemic evidence. CK-MB and LDH are less specific.
CK-MB rises 4–8 h after infarction, peaks ~24 h and normalises by 48–72 h (useful for reinfarction). Myoglobin rises earliest but is non-specific.
The longest delay in STEMI care is the patient's delay in calling for help, longest in the elderly, women and diabetics; system delays are now short.
ST elevation resolving < 50% at 60–90 min after fibrinolysis with ongoing pain is failed reperfusion: immediate rescue PCI. Repeat lysis is ineffective.
PCI vs CABG in multivessel disease depends on anatomy (SYNTAX), diabetes, LV function and chance of complete revascularisation: a heart-team decision.
When antegrade wiring of a CTO fails, a retrograde approach through collaterals is an option. CTO-PCI relieves angina; no proven mortality benefit.
PCI to a degenerated vein graft risks distal embolisation and no-reflow, so use an embolic protection device. LIMA grafts outlast vein grafts (> 90% vs ~50% at 10 years).
Days–weeks after catheterisation: livedo, blue toes, AKI, eosinophilia and high ESR = cholesterol atheroembolism. Contrast nephropathy starts within 48–72 h without eosinophilia.
Claudication with night pain eased by dependency is PAD; ABPI < 0.9 confirms it (< 0.4 critical). Calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise the ABPI.
Supervised exercise to near-maximal claudication is first line (NICE CG147). His main risk is MI or stroke; add clopidogrel and a statin. Few progress to limb loss.
Distal limb ischaemia with tapering small-artery occlusions in a young smoker is Buerger disease; complete tobacco abstinence is the only effective treatment.
Varicose veins are commoner in women, but chronic venous insufficiency with oedema is slightly commoner in men. Venous ulcers affect only 1–2% of adults.
The great saphenous vein, from the medial foot to the saphenofemoral junction, is the longest vein; it is the usual CABG conduit and the commonest site of varicosities.
A medial malleolar ulcer with haemosiderin pigment, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema after DVT is venous; treat with compression once ABPI is adequate.
NICE: lifestyle advice comes first for raised CV risk; atorvastatin 20 mg is then offered at QRISK3 ≥ 10% as a shared decision, so it is the least urgent step.
Invasive coronary angiography is the reference standard and allows PCI. NICE uses CT coronary angiography first, then functional imaging if non-diagnostic.
Fibrinolysis is indicated within 12 h of STEMI onset when PCI is not possible within 120 min; it works best in the first 3 h.
Painful blue toes with livedo but palpable pulses after anticoagulation or instrumentation is cholesterol embolism; it may also cause AKI and eosinophilia.
Lipids, smoking, hypertension and high homocysteine are risk factors. Folic acid lowers homocysteine and is not a risk factor.
Typical angina with exercise ST depression but normal angiogram is cardiac syndrome X (microvascular angina), commoner in women. Prinzmetal gives ST elevation at rest.
ACS dose of enoxaparin is 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (once daily if CrCl < 30). 40 mg daily is prophylaxis; fondaparinux 2.5 mg is preferred if no early angiography.
Treat an angina attack with sublingual GTN; call an ambulance if pain persists 5 min after the second dose. Beta-blockers or CCBs prevent attacks.
The inferior wall is seen by II, III and aVF (usually RCA). Septal = V1–V2, anterior = V3–V4, lateral = I, aVL, V5–V6.
Posterior MI mirrors in V1–V2: tall R, ST depression and upright T; V7–V9 show ST elevation. Treat as STEMI (circumflex or RCA).
Reperfusion is indicated for ischaemic pain with ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads, new LBBB or true posterior MI. ST depression alone is not an indication.
Septal, free-wall and papillary rupture are early complications (2–7 days). Dressler syndrome, LV aneurysm, mural thrombus and heart failure come weeks later.
Circumflex occlusion gives lateral ST elevation (I, aVL, V5–V6), often with posterior changes, and is the infarct most often 'silent' on the ECG.
At 20 min the earliest diagnostic sign is ST elevation (after hyperacute T waves). Troponin may still be normal and Q waves take hours.
With true aspirin allergy, use clopidogrel (a P2Y12 inhibitor) as the antiplatelet, plus anticoagulation and reperfusion. Warfarin and dipyridamole have no role.
Early-morning rest pain with transient ST elevation, no troponin rise and normal coronaries is vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: treat with CCBs and nitrates.
Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) is due to RCA occlusion in ~80%. Check V4R for RV infarction: give fluids and avoid nitrates.
Inferior STEMI with cardiogenic shock: emergency PCI of the culprit artery is the only intervention that improves survival (SHOCK). Nitrates and beta-blockers worsen hypotension.
Transient ST elevation with near-normal coronaries is vasospasm: a CCB (diltiazem/nifedipine) with nitrates and stopping smoking. Non-selective beta-blockers may worsen spasm.
Resting ST–T changes (LVH strain, LBBB, digoxin, WPW, pacing) make exercise ECG uninterpretable; use functional imaging or CT coronary angiography.
Stable NSTEMI already on aspirin, nitrate and LMWH: load a P2Y12 inhibitor to complete DAPT, then angiography within 24 h. Lysis is harmful without ST elevation.
ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression in aVL is acute inferior STEMI. Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression.
Claudication (ABPI 0.6): stop smoking, statin, antiplatelet and supervised exercise; add cilostazol or naftidrofuryl if needed. Revascularise only if lifestyle-limiting or critical.
Anterior STEMI within 1 h: aspirin, potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor/prasugrel), anticoagulation and immediate primary PCI.
In ACS, glucose > 11 mmol/L is treated with a dose-adjusted IV insulin infusion (NICE CG130). Stop metformin around angiography and sulfonylureas acutely.
Chest pain with bradycardia and hypotension suggests inferior/RV MI; the RCA supplies the AV node and RV. Nodal block here is usually transient and atropine-responsive.
ST elevation in I and aVL is a high lateral infarct (circumflex or first diagonal). Anteroseptal = V1–V4; inferior = II, III, aVF.
NICE: CT coronary angiography is first line for suspected angina; functional imaging if non-diagnostic. Exercise ECG is no longer used for diagnosis.
Troponin stays raised 7–14 days, so for reinfarction at day 4 CK-MB (normal by 2–3 days) is more useful; a new hs-troponin rise > 20% is also used.
Bicuspid aortic valve has an associated aortopathy and raises dissection risk. Others: hypertension (commonest), Marfan, Loeys–Dietz, coarctation, Turner, pregnancy, cocaine.
CT angiography of the whole aorta confirms dissection in a stable patient; TOE if unstable. Chest X-ray and transthoracic echo cannot exclude it.
Type A dissection (ascending aorta) kills 1–2%/hour untreated: emergency surgery after IV beta-blocker BP/HR control. Type B is usually medical.
Proximal dissection can rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade, a leading cause of death; also acute AR, coronary occlusion and branch ischaemia.
Sudden severe chest pain in a hypertensive with no MI on ECG/troponin: exclude aortic dissection before antithrombotics or thrombolysis, which could be fatal.
An early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation; in Marfan syndrome aortic root dilatation stretches the valve ring. MVP gives a click and late systolic murmur.
Diabetes is consistently linked to fewer and slower-growing AAAs. Smoking is the strongest risk factor; also male sex, age, family history and hypertension.
Stopping smoking slows AAA growth and lowers rupture risk; drugs (ACEi, beta-blocker, statin) have not been shown to slow growth.
Pregnancy (third trimester/peripartum) predisposes to dissection through medial hormonal change and high cardiac output; this woman had no Marfan features.
Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, due to FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations: tall, ectopia lentis, aortic root dilatation and MVP. Sarcomere genes cause HCM.
A pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture held only by adventitia or surrounding tissue (after puncture, surgery, trauma). A true aneurysm involves all three layers.
Degenerative aortic aneurysms are several times commoner in men, so female sex is not a risk factor. Age, smoking, hypertension and family history are.
Aortic root aneurysm with hypertelorism, bifid uvula and familial sudden death is Loeys–Dietz (TGFBR1/2); aneurysms dissect smaller, so repair earlier than Marfan.
Uncomplicated type B dissection (beyond the left subclavian) is treated medically with IV beta-blockade. Malperfusion, rupture or expansion need repair; any ascending involvement needs surgery.
Ascending aortic dilatation: GCA, Takayasu, syphilis, spondyloarthritis, Marfan/Loeys–Dietz/EDS, bicuspid valve. SLE is not a recognised cause.
A 3.0–3.5 cm AAA is monitored with ultrasound while treating risk factors; repair at ≥ 5.5 cm, growth > 1 cm/year or symptoms. EVAR is an alternative to open repair.
Tearing back pain, severe hypertension, new AR and widened mediastinum is proximal dissection: IV beta-blocker, then nitroprusside, urgent TOE/CT and surgery.
One-off ultrasound AAA screening is offered to men 65–75 who have ever smoked (all men at 65 in the UK); it reduces aneurysm deaths.
A young woman with prior systemic illness, chest pain and an absent radial pulse has Takayasu arteritis (large-vessel vasculitis); diagnose by CT/MR angiography, treat with steroids.
After ACS with a drug-eluting stent, DAPT continues ~12 months; stopping clopidogrel at 3 weeks risks fatal stent thrombosis. Defer elective surgery (≥ 6, ideally 12 months).
Coronary disease is the commonest cause of HFrEF; about half of heart failure is HFpEF, and 1-year mortality is still ~10–30%.
Orthopnoea, pink frothy sputum, crackles, raised JVP, oedema and cardiomegaly is acute decompensated heart failure. COPD/asthma give wheeze without a raised JVP.
Congestion in acute heart failure is treated with an IV loop diuretic (furosemide), sitting up, oxygen if hypoxic and nitrates if BP allows. Diltiazem is negatively inotropic.
Heart failure causes arrhythmias, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (ACEi/MRA) and raised urea (cardiorenal). Hyperlipidaemia is a cause of the underlying CAD, not a complication.
Echocardiography is key: EF (HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF), valves, wall motion, pericardium and filling pressures. Angiography comes later if ischaemia is suspected.
Spironolactone (MRA) improves symptoms and survival in HFrEF (RALES). Flecainide raises mortality in structural heart disease; NSAIDs worsen fluid retention.
If ACEi/ARB/ARNI cannot be used (renal impairment, hyperkalaemia), hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate reduces HFrEF mortality and does not raise potassium.
In HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) reduce heart-failure hospitalisation and CV death; diuretics for congestion and treat comorbidities.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy during pregnancy: beta-blocker and loop diuretic (hydralazine/nitrate if needed). ACEi, ARB, ARNI and MRA are unsafe before delivery.
ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HFrEF mortality. Digoxin reduced admissions but not mortality (DIG trial).
In older patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, exclude coronary disease before calling it non-ischaemic, as revascularisation may help.
A heart-failure patient on only furosemide and aspirin lacks prognostic therapy: start an ACE inhibitor (also treats her BP), then beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2i.
Biventricular failure with cardiomegaly and global hypokinesia (EF 25–30%) in a young woman is dilated cardiomyopathy. Restrictive disease keeps systolic function.
ACE inhibitors (or ARB/ARNI) reduce HFrEF mortality and remodelling and are a cornerstone with beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2i. Non-DHP CCBs worsen HFrEF.
Evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) cut HFrEF mortality by ~a third; start low when euvolaemic and titrate slowly.
Loop diuretics relieve congestion and symptoms but do not improve survival; use the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolaemic.
DCM predisposes to AF and ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death is common; consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy.
Stasis in a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle (and atria in AF) causes mural thrombus and embolism; anticoagulate for AF or documented LV thrombus.
S3 reflects rapid filling of a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle with high filling pressure (gallop rhythm). Opening snap = MS; pericardial knock = constriction.
DCM causes: alcohol, haemochromatosis, myocarditis, genetic, peripartum, anthracyclines, tachycardia. Hypertension causes concentric LVH and HFpEF, so is least likely.
Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) mutations classically cause HCM. Alcohol, pregnancy and persistent tachycardia cause DCM (the last two may reverse).
With COPD and IHD together, a gallop rhythm (S3) is the most specific sign that breathlessness is from LV failure with high filling pressure.
By LVEF: HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥ 50% with raised filling pressures. High-output failure is a separate category.
ACC/AHA stages: A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C structural disease with symptoms, D refractory. NYHA classes grade symptoms separately.
CRT (biventricular pacing) for HFrEF with EF ≤ 35%, LBBB and QRS ≥ 150 ms despite optimal therapy restores synchrony and improves EF and survival.
Long-standing hypertension causes LVH: tall voltages (S V1 + R V5/6 > 35 mm) with lateral ST–T 'strain'. RVH suggests pulmonary hypertension.
Exertional fatigue and syncope with familial sudden death in a teenager is HCM, the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes; ECG and echo first.
The HCM murmur comes from dynamic LVOT obstruction (septal hypertrophy plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve); it does not radiate to the carotids.
Echo confirms HCM: unexplained wall thickness ≥ 15 mm (often septal), SAM and an outflow gradient. MRI and Holter refine risk.
Syncope in HCM is usually from ventricular arrhythmia or a surge in outflow obstruction; unexplained syncope is a major sudden-death risk factor favouring an ICD.
Orthopnoea is breathlessness soon after lying flat (venous redistribution), relieved by sitting up. PND wakes the patient after hours of sleep.
RV infarction with inferior MI: hypotension, raised JVP, hepatomegaly and clear lungs. Give IV fluids and avoid nitrates and diuretics.
Frank–Starling: stroke volume and output rise with ventricular filling (preload) up to a plateau; in heart failure the curve is flat, so extra filling causes congestion.
Low output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system: salt/water retention, vasoconstriction and remodelling — the targets of ACEi/ARNI, MRAs and beta-blockers.
DCM is dilatation (often biventricular) with thin walls and systolic dysfunction not explained by loading or coronary disease. Septal thickening = HCM.
Heavy alcohol (> 80 g/day for years) is a common, reversible cause of DCM. SCN5A mutations cause Brugada and long QT3.
HCM: asymmetric LVH with disproportionate septal thickening (septum/posterior wall > 1.3), myocyte disarray and dynamic outflow obstruction in ~two-thirds.
Transplantation is for stage D heart failure with poor quality of life despite optimal drug and device therapy and no contraindications; LVAD is an alternative.
Sudden death in HCM is from VT/VF arising in fibrotic myocardium, often on exertion; risk is scored (ESC HCM Risk-SCD) and high-risk patients get an ICD.
Beta-blockers reduce total and sudden death in HFrEF (as do MRAs and ARNI); consider an ICD if EF stays ≤ 35%. Verapamil is harmful; screen the family.
ST elevation, normal coronaries and apical ballooning in a postmenopausal woman after emotional stress is takotsubo cardiomyopathy; LV function usually recovers.
Loop diuretics relieve symptoms but do not improve survival. Bisoprolol, enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone and SGLT2i reduce mortality.
Heart failure with high EF and a pseudo-infarct ECG (low voltages) in an elderly woman suggests restrictive (amyloid) cardiomyopathy.
Thyroid disease causes heart failure: thyrotoxicosis gives high-output failure and AF; hypothyroidism a dilated heart. Check TFTs in all new heart failure.
HCM is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance (MYH7, MYBPC3); screen first-degree relatives with ECG and echo ± genetic testing.
Hypertensive pulmonary oedema: oxygen/CPAP, IV nitrates and IV furosemide. Dobutamine is for cardiogenic shock and only raises oxygen demand here.
Anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is cumulative, dose-dependent and largely irreversible. Alcohol, haemochromatosis and thyroid DCM can improve.
Pulsus alternans (alternating strong and weak beats in regular rhythm, independent of respiration) indicates severe LV systolic dysfunction.
S4 needs atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it cannot occur in AF. S3, reversed splitting (LBBB) and Kussmaul's sign all fit.
Thick 'sparkling' myocardium with biatrial enlargement and preserved EF suggests amyloidosis: first exclude AL with serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains.
NSVT in heart failure predicts higher mortality, but antiarrhythmic suppression does not help (class I harmful, CAST); optimise HF therapy and electrolytes.
Comfortable at rest but symptoms on less than ordinary activity (e.g. a short walk) is NYHA class III.
Heart failure with warm peripheries, tachycardia, exophthalmos and tremor is thyrotoxic high-output failure: beta-blocker, diuretic and treat the thyroid.
In HFrEF angiotensin II, noradrenaline, natriuretic peptides and TNF rise, but SR calcium uptake falls (SERCA2a down-regulated), impairing relaxation.
BNP rises with age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, sepsis and ACS. Obesity lowers BNP, so a 'normal' value does not exclude heart failure in obese patients.
Correcting hypoxaemia relieves hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and lowers RV afterload. High PEEP, large tidal volumes and hypercapnia raise it.
No drug has convincingly reduced mortality in HFpEF; SGLT2i reduce the combined endpoint mainly via fewer admissions. Treat congestion and comorbidities.
'Warm and wet': start an IV loop diuretic (at least the oral dose). Inotropes are for 'cold' low-output states; ultrafiltration for diuretic resistance.
Nesiritide (recombinant BNP) lowers wedge pressure faster than nitrates but causes hypotension and did not improve outcomes (ASCEND-HF).
In cardiogenic shock output falls and sympathetic vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance (cool peripheries); mixed venous saturation falls.
Beta-blocker or ACEi first gives similar outcomes (CIBIS III); start all four pillars early in low doses and titrate to target.
Adding an ARB or aliskiren to ACEi + MRA raises hyperkalaemia and renal risk without benefit; SGLT2i need caution in type 1 diabetes (ketoacidosis), so no change.
Primary-prevention ICD: LVEF ≤ 35% despite ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy, NYHA II–III and reasonable survival. Recheck EF after myocarditis or peripartum disease.
Spironolactone cut HFrEF mortality by ~30% (RALES), eplerenone in milder HF (EMPHASIS-HF). Diuretics relieve congestion but activate RAAS.
In chronic HF digoxin is given 62.5–250 µg daily without loading; levels only if toxicity, renal impairment or interactions. It reduces admissions, not mortality.
Heart-failure CXR: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, bat-wing oedema, Kerley B lines, effusions, fissure fluid. The left lung has no horizontal fissure.
Breathless at rest with gross oedema: relieve congestion first with a loop diuretic; start/titrate ACEi and beta-blocker once less congested.
ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalaemia (less aldosterone), not hypokalaemia; also cough, angioedema, first-dose hypotension and AKI. Check U&E before and after dose changes.
An ICD is the only proven way to prevent sudden death in HCM: after aborted arrest (as here) or when the ESC 5-year risk is ≥ 6%.
Ascites, tender liver, jaundice, AF, oedema, orthopnoea and systolic JVP waves (TR) mean congestive (biventricular) failure. Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP.
Decompensated aortic stenosis first raises LA and pulmonary venous pressure, giving bibasal crackles; raised JVP and oedema follow only with right failure.
Venous hypertension causes upper-lobe diversion; 'lower-lobe diversion' is not a sign. Cardiomegaly, effusions, alveolar oedema and Kerley B lines are typical.
Nausea, anorexia and yellow vision/halos are digoxin toxicity, promoted by hypokalaemia, CKD and interacting drugs; give Digifab for life-threatening toxicity.
Acute LV failure (likely MI) raises pulmonary capillary pressure, causing hydrostatic oedema, hypoxaemia and hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis). Permeability = ARDS.
Exertional breathlessness with an S3 suggests heart failure; a raised BNP/NT-proBNP supports it and NICE then arranges echo (within 2 or 6 weeks).
A perihilar bat-wing pattern is alveolar oedema; in a breathless smoker the likeliest cause is LV failure. TR causes systemic, not pulmonary, congestion.
Syncope during exertion is a red flag (HCM, anomalous coronaries, long QT, ARVC, WPW): ECG and echo, and no competitive sport until cleared.
EF 38% after heart failure (stage C) needs prognostic therapy: ACEi (or ARB/ARNI) plus beta-blocker, then MRA and SGLT2i, even if now asymptomatic.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (EF < 45% late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum): about half recover fully; recurrence in later pregnancies is common.
HFrEF still NYHA III on ACEi, beta-blocker and diuretic: add an MRA (spironolactone) with K⁺/renal monitoring; SGLT2i and ARNI follow.
Multiply transfused patients develop iron-overload cardiomyopathy: check ferritin and transferrin saturation, then cardiac MRI T2*; chelation can reverse it.
BNP < 100 pg/mL (NT-proBNP < 300 acutely) has a high negative predictive value: acute heart failure is unlikely, so look for another cause.
BNP causes natriuresis, vasodilatation and inhibits RAAS and sympathetic activity. Sacubitril raises natriuretic peptides by blocking neprilysin.
BNP/NT-proBNP is secreted mainly by ventricular myocytes in response to stretch; ANP comes from the atria.
BNP can be raised without LV failure in COPD (RV strain), PE, AF, sepsis, CKD, cirrhosis and age > 70. Obesity and HF drugs lower it.
Pulmonary flow murmur, fixed wide S2 splitting and incomplete RBBB (RSR' in V1) with plethoric lungs is a secundum ASD.
About half of patients with coarctation have a bicuspid aortic valve; both are common in Turner syndrome.
Hypertension in a young man with an arm BP difference suggests coarctation at or near the left subclavian origin (left arm lower). Check radiofemoral delay.
Inferior rib notching (ribs 3–8) from dilated intercostal collaterals is classic of coarctation, rarely before age 8; the '3 sign' is another clue.
Significant coarctation (gradient ≥ 20 mmHg or hypertension) is repaired: stenting in suitable adults, surgery in infants. Lifelong follow-up for recoarctation.
A small secundum ASD without pulmonary hypertension is well tolerated in pregnancy (mWHO II); routine follow-up is enough.
Isolated secundum ASD has very low endocarditis risk; prophylaxis is not indicated (NICE never routinely; ESC only for high-risk lesions).
In ASD the shunt keeps RV volume high throughout respiration, so S2 is widely split with a fixed interval. Paradoxical splitting = LBBB or severe AS.
Secundum ASD typically shows RSR' in V1 (incomplete RBBB) with right axis deviation; left axis deviation suggests a primum defect.
Eisenmenger develops in a minority of large unrepaired shunts (< 10% of adult ASDs); a small secundum ASD carries low risk.
Exertional collapse with deep cyanosis in congenital heart disease is a tetralogy of Fallot spell (RVOT spasm increases right-to-left shunt).
Eisenmenger syndrome: shunt reversal causes cyanosis, clubbing and erythrocytosis; life expectancy is markedly reduced and pregnancy is very high-risk.
A small restrictive VSD gives a loud harsh pansystolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge despite a trivial shunt (maladie de Roger).
Clubbing and cyanosis of toes but not fingers (differential cyanosis) is PDA with pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal.
Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies damage the fetal conduction system, causing congenital complete heart block; monitor the fetal heart from 16 weeks.
Limb ischaemia in a young woman with a childhood murmur suggests paradoxical embolism through an ASD/PFO; echo with bubble study shows the shunt.
Fixed S2 splitting with flow murmurs and a stroke in a young adult suggests paradoxical embolism across an ASD; confirm with bubble echo and consider closure.
A small VSD causes no overload or pulmonary hypertension; its main long-term risk is infective endocarditis. Many small muscular VSDs close spontaneously.
VSD gives a harsh holosystolic murmur at the mid/lower left sternal border. ASD = pulmonary flow murmur; PDA = continuous machinery murmur.
Significant PDA in a preterm infant is closed medically with a COX inhibitor (ibuprofen/indomethacin) or paracetamol; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open.
VSD complications: heart failure, Eisenmenger, aortic regurgitation, endocarditis. AF reflects atrial overload (ASD, mitral disease), not VSD.
Thyrotoxic AF: a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) controls rate and adrenergic symptoms; antithyroid treatment restores sinus rhythm. Amiodarone worsens thyroid disease.
Digoxin effect is down-sloping ('reverse tick') ST depression with T flattening and short QT; toxicity shows as brady/junctional rhythms, ectopics or atrial tachycardia with block.
Hypertension is the commonest condition underlying AF (atrial pressure load); others: IHD, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid, alcohol, obesity, sleep apnoea.
Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat; AV-nodal, often benign, rarely needs pacing. Mobitz II (infranodal) progresses and needs pacing.
AF is treated with rate control, rhythm control (cardioversion, drugs, ablation) and anticoagulation. An ICD treats ventricular arrhythmias only.
AF at 120/min with hypertension and IHD: a beta-blocker (metoprolol) controls rate, BP and angina. He also needs a DOAC rather than aspirin.
Fusion beats prove AV dissociation and are diagnostic of VT; collapse means pulseless VT, treated like VF with immediate defibrillation.
A rate of 36/min with P waves independent of QRS is complete heart block; after anterior MI it is infranodal (septal necrosis) and needs pacing.
AF with shock (BP 70/50) needs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation, with heparin, whatever the AF duration.
CHA2DS2-VASc = 6 (age ≥ 75 ×2, female, HTN, diabetes, HF): long-term anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC (rivaroxaban/apixaban). Antiplatelets are not adequate.
Symptomatic AF despite drugs in an older HF patient: 'pace and ablate' (pacemaker then AV-node ablation) gives permanent rate control; PV isolation is the rhythm option.
Rate control uses beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil or digoxin. Amiodarone is mainly for rhythm control and too toxic for long-term rate control.
CHA2DS2-VASc: heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, stroke/TIA, vascular disease, female sex. Obesity raises AF risk but is not in the score.
PR > 200 ms: AV-nodal drugs, hypokalaemia, rheumatic fever, Lyme disease, inferior MI, fibrosis. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT, not the PR.
The key complication of AF is ischaemic stroke from left atrial appendage thrombus (risk ×5); hence CHA2DS2-VASc and anticoagulation.
Antipsychotics (risperidone, haloperidol) block hERG channels, prolong QT and cause torsades. Treat with IV magnesium and stop the drug.
Irregular cannon a waves mean AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT); regular ones occur in junctional rhythms. AF abolishes a waves.
Orthodromic AVRT is narrow and AV-node-dependent, so adenosine terminates it. In pre-excited AF (irregular, broad) AV-nodal blockers are dangerous.
Rapid irregular palpitations in an older person are most likely AF (prevalence ~10% over 80); confirm with an ECG during symptoms.
Constant PR with sudden dropped P waves is Mobitz II: infranodal, progresses to complete block and causes Stokes–Adams attacks — permanent pacemaker.
Sick sinus syndrome: sinus bradycardia, pauses, SA block, often with AF/atrial tachycardia (tachy–brady). VT is not a feature.
Age ≥ 75 (2) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 5: high stroke risk; offer a DOAC.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (modified Valsalva), then adenosine 6–12–18 mg rapid bolus. DC shock if unstable.
Permanent pacing for symptomatic bradycardia (sick sinus with syncope), Mobitz II and complete heart block. Athletes' bradycardia is physiological.
Alcohol triggers AF ('holiday heart') and heavy intake raises AF incidence; abstinence reduces recurrence. It also causes dilated cardiomyopathy.
Heart block plus erythema nodosum suggests sarcoidosis: granulomas in the septum/conduction system; confirm with cardiac MRI or FDG-PET.
Broad QRS with rSR' ('M') in V1–V2 and slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6 is RBBB. LBBB gives a broad QS in V1 and notched R in V6.
Sinus bradycardia, first-degree and Wenckebach block are physiological in asymptomatic athletes; no tests or restriction needed.
A prolonged sinus node recovery time after overdrive pacing (1800 ms) with low intrinsic rate means intrinsic SA node disease.
Reversible SA node dysfunction: hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised ICP, drugs, hyperkalaemia, vagal tone. Radiation causes permanent fibrosis.
Tachy–brady syndrome includes AF/flutter; atrial enlargement (and age, prior stroke, LV dysfunction) adds embolic risk. A pacemaker does not remove it.
Decremental conduction (slower conduction at faster rates) is shown by atrial pacing at shorter cycle lengths with a lengthening AH interval until Wenckebach.
The AV node lies near the aortic annulus, so AVR/TAVI can cause complete heart block; pace permanently if it persists beyond ~5–7 days.
Constant PR then sudden dropped P waves with syncope is Mobitz II; it tends to progress to complete block, so implant a permanent pacemaker.
Nocturnal Mobitz I in an asymptomatic athlete is high vagal tone; it resolves with exercise. Reassure.
Monitoring depends on symptom frequency: Holter for daily symptoms, event recorder for every few days, implantable loop recorder for rare episodes.
Atrial premature complexes are common and benign in a normal heart; reassure and reduce caffeine/alcohol. Beta-blocker only if troublesome.
Sudden loss of the delta wave on exercise shows a pathway with a long refractory period, so low risk of pre-excited AF degenerating to VF.
Recent-onset AF converts with DC shock, flecainide or amiodarone. Adenosine only transiently blocks the AV node and does not convert AF.
AF with heart failure, hypertension, vascular disease and age ≥ 75 (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 5): oral anticoagulation is class I. Flecainide is contraindicated.
Rhythm control did not improve survival (AFFIRM) and asymptomatic recurrence is common, so anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VASc, not apparent sinus rhythm.
Irregular very fast broad complexes of varying shape are pre-excited AF; with collapse give immediate DC shock. AV-nodal blockers can precipitate VF.
Irregularly irregular broad complexes with varying width and RR < 250 ms is AF conducting down an accessory pathway. VT and AVRT are regular.
A regular broad ventricular rhythm at 60–110/min soon after thrombolysis is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a benign reperfusion marker.
Torsades from methadone + erythromycin persisting after magnesium: raise the rate with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing to shorten QT. Amiodarone worsens it.
AV dissociation (independent P waves, fusion or capture beats) is diagnostic of VT. Prior MI, QRS > 160 ms and chest-lead concordance also favour VT.
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (rate rises on inspiration, falls on expiration) is normal, especially in the young; all beats are sinus, so reassure.
2:1 block with narrow QRS in a sleeping young athlete is almost certainly vagally mediated AV-nodal block; infranodal block usually has broad QRS.
Atropine removes vagal tone at SA and AV nodes, raising the rate and restoring 1:1 conduction in nodal block; in infranodal block it may worsen the ratio.
Parkinsonian tremor artefact (4–6 Hz) can mimic flutter, AF or VT; regular QRS complexes seen through it confirm sinus rhythm, so no treatment.
Saw-tooth waves in II, III, aVF with 2:1 conduction is typical flutter; its stroke risk equals AF, and CHA2DS2-VASc is high, so anticoagulate before ablation.
A negative delta wave and LBBB-like QRS in V1 indicate a right-sided accessory pathway; a positive delta in V1 indicates a left-sided pathway.
A wide ventricular rhythm at 75/min soon after successful lysis in a well patient is accelerated idioventricular rhythm: observe. Suppression is harmful.
Sinus pauses with absent P waves plus bradycardia in an older person is sick sinus syndrome. In AV block P waves are present but not conducted.
If vagal manoeuvres fail, adenosine (6 mg rapid bolus, then 12 and 18 mg) terminates AV-node-dependent SVT; verapamil if asthmatic.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: after vagal manoeuvres give adenosine, which ends AVNRT/AVRT or unmasks flutter waves. Cardiovert only if adverse features.
PR > 200 ms with every P conducted is first-degree AV block (ageing, vagal tone, AV-nodal drugs, inferior MI); no treatment needed alone.
Dropped P waves with a fixed PR in conducted beats is Mobitz II: infranodal, can progress abruptly to complete block, so pace permanently.
Atrial rate 300/min with ventricular rate 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 block; suspect it in any regular narrow tachycardia near 150/min.
Synchronised DC cardioversion restores sinus rhythm in > 90% of flutter (drugs work poorly); anticoagulate as for AF. CTI ablation prevents recurrence.
Paroxysmal palpitations with sweating: check TFTs, metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma), ambulatory ECG and echo. An upper GI study has no role.
Irregular tachycardia without P waves is AF; first-line rate control in a stable patient is a beta-blocker (bisoprolol). Flecainide is for rhythm control.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (carotid massage if young, no bruit); then adenosine, or verapamil if asthmatic.
Syncope during exercise is a cardiac red flag (HCM, long QT, WPW, Brugada, ARVC); a 12-lead ECG is the essential first test.
Brief self-terminating AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 0 and a normal heart needs no anticoagulation; antiplatelets are never used for AF stroke prevention.
CHA2DS2-VASc 5: oral anticoagulation. After ACS with AF: brief triple therapy (≤ 1 week), then DOAC + clopidogrel to 12 months, then DOAC alone.
Weight loss, fatigue and new AF in a young woman suggest hyperthyroidism: check TSH and free T4 (recommended in all new AF).
AF < 48 h can be cardioverted once heparin is started. Prior MI contraindicates flecainide, so use DC cardioversion (or amiodarone).
Infrequent paroxysmal AF in a normal heart: 'pill-in-the-pocket' flecainide with an AV-nodal blocker. Sotalol is contraindicated in asthma.
The a wave is atrial contraction, so it is absent in AF. Cannon a waves = AV dissociation; large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation.
Rapid SVT ending in a long pause with dizziness/syncope is tachy–brady sick sinus syndrome: permanent pacemaker, then rate-control drugs safely.
Ischaemic stroke with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 6): lifelong anticoagulation, DOAC preferred (or warfarin INR 2–3), started within days depending on infarct size.
Flutter waves ~250/min with 2:1 block in a stable patient: rate control first with IV metoprolol, then anticoagulation and elective cardioversion/ablation.
Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat is Mobitz I (AV-nodal, benign): observe and review AV-nodal drugs if asymptomatic.
Complete heart block after anterior MI is infranodal with an unreliable escape rhythm: pace (temporary, then assess permanent) even if BP is stable.
Regular saw-tooth waves ~300/min with a QRS after every fourth is atrial flutter with 4:1 block; decongestants and lung disease are triggers.
Older patient with dilated LA, now rate-controlled and asymptomatic: continue rate control plus long-term anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 3).
Short PR, delta wave and wide QRS is pre-excitation (WPW); palpitations or syncope warrant an EP study and pathway ablation.
Congenital long QT is most often loss of potassium-channel function (KCNQ1 LQT1, hERG LQT2); treat with nadolol/propranolol and avoid QT drugs.
AF lasting > 7 days (or needing cardioversion after 7 days) is persistent; paroxysmal ends within 7 days, permanent means rhythm control abandoned.
In complete heart block the varying AV interval makes S1 intensity vary (with intermittent cannon a waves). Stop bisoprolol and pace.
Bradycardia with an adverse feature (syncope): IV atropine 500 µg, repeat to 3 mg; then transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline/adrenaline infusion.
CHA2DS2-VASc 5 (age 75 = 2, female, prior TIA = 2): anticoagulate (DOAC); AF during acute illness often recurs. Aspirin is not used.
Adenosine is given 6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg by rapid bolus with flush; repeating 6 mg rarely works. Verapamil if adenosine fails.
LBBB occurs with IHD, hypertension/LVH, AS, cardiomyopathy and conduction fibrosis. Secundum ASD causes RBBB with right axis deviation.
QTc 500 ms is prolonged (high torsades risk); hypokalaemia (flat T, U waves) is a common cause. Hypercalcaemia and digoxin shorten the QT.
Torsades needs a long QT: TCAs, SAH, hypothermia, congenital LQTS, low K/Mg/Ca. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT. Treat with IV magnesium 2 g.
AF with HFrEF and brittle asthma: rate-limiting CCBs are negatively inotropic and beta-blockers are precluded, so digoxin is used.
CHB after inferior MI is nodal (narrow escape, atropine-responsive, usually resolves), so pacing is not needed if stable; after anterior MI it is.
Penicillin-sensitive streptococcal native-valve IE: IV benzylpenicillin 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin if uncomplicated). Vancomycin is for allergy.
Symptomatic severe AS (area < 1 cm², mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg) with EF < 50% needs AVR — surgical or TAVI by heart team. No drug improves outlook.
An opening snap after S2, with a loud S1 and apical mid-diastolic rumble, is mitral stenosis; the shorter the S2–snap interval, the more severe the stenosis.
Significant chronic AR gives a wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic), so 120/95 mmHg argues against it. Acute AR may have a near-normal pulse pressure.
Exertional dyspnoea and PND with an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation (rheumatic or prolapse in the young); echo confirms.
Early diastolic murmur with wide pulse pressure is AR; the apical rumble is an Austin Flint murmur, told from MS by a normal S1 and no opening snap.
Echo (TTE/TOE) and catheterisation define a chronic valve lesion; cardiac enzymes detect myocardial necrosis and say nothing about valve disease.
Loud P2, RV heave and RVH with functional TR (normal leaflets) means pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure; then find its cause.
A displaced apex with a soft S1 in rheumatic disease is mitral regurgitation (LV volume overload). MS gives a loud S1 and tapping undisplaced apex.
Long-standing MS causes pulmonary hypertension and RV failure (raised JVP, RV heave, hepatomegaly, oedema); this indicates valvotomy or surgery.
In MS the apex is undisplaced and tapping (a palpable loud S1) because the LV is protected from overload.
Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud (even palpable) P2, often with an RV heave. The opening snap and loud S1 come from the mitral valve itself.
Balloon mitral commissurotomy: symptomatic MS (area ≤ 1.5 cm²) with pliable non-calcified leaflets, ≤ mild MR and no LA thrombus on TOE.
In MS with sinus rhythm, atrial contraction causes pre-systolic accentuation of the rumble; it disappears when AF develops.
A basal systolic thrill with an ejection murmur in an elderly man is most likely calcific aortic stenosis; echo grades severity.
Pulse pressure 120 mmHg with significant AR gives hyperdynamic signs: collapsing pulse, Corrigan, de Musset (head nodding), Quincke and Duroziez.
Symptomatic severe AS has ~50% 2-year mortality without replacement; at prohibitive surgical risk, refer for TAVI (heart-team assessment).
Ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; angina, dyspnoea and syncope signal severe disease.
Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, with a raised JVP and large v waves, is tricuspid regurgitation.
Transthoracic echo with Doppler confirms AS and grades it (velocity, gradient, area) with LV function; angiography is done before surgery.
In MS the enlarged LA straightens the left heart border, gives a double right border and splays (widens) the carina; upper-lobe diversion and Kerley B lines.
Ectopia lentis, pectus, high palate and hypermobility suggest Marfan syndrome, commonly with MVP; aortic root dilatation is the dangerous lesion.
Mitral murmurs are loudest at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position; MR is pansystolic, radiates to the axilla, louder in expiration.
Mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse (Barlow); standing/Valsalva bring the click earlier, squatting delays it.
MS signs: malar flush, AF, tapping apex, loud S1, opening snap, RV heave. A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.
MVP is systolic displacement of a leaflet > 2 mm into the LA; most are asymptomatic and need no drugs, but echo follow-up is advised.
Bioprosthetic valves degenerate after ~10 years (earlier in mitral position); a new apical diastolic murmur means prosthetic MS. Exclude endocarditis; redo or valve-in-valve.
Dyspnoea, AF and haemoptysis with an apical diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, usually a late consequence of childhood rheumatic fever.
Severe MR with pulmonary oedema and adequate BP: IV afterload reduction (nitroprusside/nitrates) increases forward flow; IABP if hypotensive; then surgery.
Dental prophylaxis (AHA/ESC) only for highest risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD. NICE does not recommend it routinely.
Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (INR ~2.5–3.5 mitral, 2.0–3.0 bileaflet aortic). DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN).
A pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo) is tricuspid regurgitation; in Marfan it may follow tricuspid prolapse.
TR (e.g. right-sided IE in drug users) gives giant v (cv) waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver. Cannon a waves mean AV dissociation.
A bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse occurs in mixed aortic valve disease with predominant AR, severe AR and HOCM. Pure AS gives a slow-rising pulse.
Severe calcific AS gives a soft or absent A2 (and reversed splitting). Pulmonary hypertension gives a loud P2; ASD gives fixed splitting.
AR arises from leaflet disease (rheumatic, IE, bicuspid) or root dilatation (Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilis). DCM causes functional MR/TR.
Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with click and soft P2; balloon valvuloplasty if severe.
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus with RA collapse is tamponade (likely malignant): urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis. Diuretics are harmful.
Positional pain, friction rub and concave ST elevation across several territories is acute pericarditis; treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.
A new raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus and hypotension days after pericarditis means tamponade; confirm with echo and drain urgently.
Echo shows the effusion, RA/RV diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC, and guides pericardiocentesis. ECG and CXR are insensitive.
Tamponade with hypotension needs urgent pericardiocentesis; diuretics, nitrates and ACEi worsen filling. Fluids only as a bridge.
In rheumatic fever, carditis and recurrence are commonest when the first attack is in young children, so young age is a bad sign; penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence.
Duke major criteria: persistently positive blood cultures (e.g. 3 sets ≥ 1 h apart) or imaging evidence of endocardial involvement. IVDU and emboli are minor.
Tamponade raises all diastolic pressures, so the JVP is high (blunted y descent); a collapsed JVP means hypovolaemia. Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds.
Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within weeks of surgery) is mostly coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus acquired peri-operatively.
Constriction causes systemic congestion (raised JVP, Kussmaul sign, early ascites, hepatomegaly) with clear lungs, so prominent breathlessness argues against it.
Myocarditis gives chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmia and raised troponin; a rub means associated pericarditis. Cardiac MRI is the key test.
Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and peaks at 5–15 years; it is rare under 3 and uncommon in adults.
Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, then T inversion. Hyperacute T waves are the earliest sign of STEMI.
Fever, weight loss, a new regurgitant murmur and splinter haemorrhages is infective endocarditis: 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, then echo.
Take ≥ 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics: they identify the organism and are a major Duke criterion; echo follows promptly.
Embolisation of vegetations, most often to the brain, makes new focal weakness an embolic stroke; image urgently and consider early surgery.
Surgery in IE: heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungi) or large vegetations with emboli. Age is not an indication.
Constriction gives a raised JVP with rapid y descent, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock and ascites. Pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of tamponade.
Right-sided congestion with a steep y descent after previous TB is constrictive pericarditis; CT/MRI shows thickening or calcification.
Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI (antimyocardial antibodies); treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.
Distant heart sounds with a newly enlarged globular silhouette after a viral illness is pericardial effusion (> 200–250 mL); echo confirms and checks for tamponade.
A to-and-fro scratchy sound in systole and diastole after a viral illness is a pericardial rub (acute viral pericarditis); treat with NSAID plus colchicine.
Acute pericarditis: high-dose aspirin or ibuprofen tapered over 1–2 weeks plus colchicine for 3 months (halves recurrence). Steroids are second line.
TB is the commonest cause of constriction worldwide; others are cardiac surgery, radiotherapy, viral/idiopathic pericarditis and connective tissue disease.
A large effusion in an older smoker suggests malignancy; a rub is often absent, echo confirms, and diuretics do not help. Drain and send cytology.
PR depression (with PR elevation in aVR) is the most specific ECG sign of pericarditis; ST elevation is diffuse, concave and without reciprocal change.
Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall > 10 mmHg) is the key bedside sign that an effusion is causing tamponade; echo confirms.
Hypotension, distended neck veins and a water-bottle heart in lung cancer is malignant tamponade, so pulsus paradoxus is expected. Kussmaul sign suggests constriction.
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness, no high-risk features: outpatient ibuprofen plus colchicine.
Pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward is acute pericarditis; with breast cancer consider malignant involvement and check echo.
Fever, pleuritic pain, rub and diffuse ST elevation weeks after MI is Dressler syndrome; early infarct pericarditis occurs within 1–3 days.
Fever and pleuritic pain 2 weeks after MI with no new ECG change is Dressler syndrome: aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine. Anticoagulation risks haemopericardium.
Chest discomfort, hypotension, raised JVP and quiet heart sounds hours after pacing suggest lead perforation with haemopericardium/tamponade.
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and low voltages weeks after MI is tamponade from a post-MI effusion: urgent echo and pericardiocentesis.
Multi-territory ST elevation with pleuritic pain in a young woman is pericarditis; a small troponin rise means myopericarditis, not ACS.
Carditis is the only rheumatic fever manifestation causing permanent damage (chronic rheumatic valve disease); arthritis, rash and chorea resolve.
MVP without regurgitation has near-population endocarditis risk. Prosthetic valves and previous IE carry the highest risk.
Viridans streptococcal native-valve IE is usually penicillin-sensitive with > 90% cure. S. aureus, prosthetic and culture-negative IE do worse.
Janeway lesions (painless palmar/plantar haemorrhagic macules from septic emboli) are characteristic of endocarditis; a minor Duke criterion.
After blood cultures, start empirical high-dose IV bactericidal antibiotics, then tailor to the organism for 4–6 weeks. Surgery only for specific indications.
Prolonged fever with a new wide pulse pressure suggests aortic valve endocarditis with acute AR; its soft short murmur is easily missed.
Jones minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR. Carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and nodules are major.
Rheumatic arthritis responds dramatically to aspirin within 24–48 h; a rapid response supports the diagnosis.
An indolent illness with anaemia and partial response to antibiotics is subacute native-valve IE, classically viridans streptococci.
Microscopic haematuria (glomerulonephritis or renal emboli) is commoner in IE than splinters, Osler nodes or Roth spots; dipstick the urine.
A new or changing regurgitant murmur with fever is the most suggestive feature of IE; new regurgitation on echo is a major Duke criterion.
In people who inject drugs, S. aureus is the commonest cause of IE, usually tricuspid with septic pulmonary emboli; cover MRSA where prevalent.
Prophylaxis only for highest risk (prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD). ASD, VSD, CABG and pacemakers do not qualify.
Immune-complex phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, rheumatoid factor. Splenic abscess is embolic (vascular), like Janeway lesions.
Definite IE (modified Duke): 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor. Three minor criteria give only 'possible' endocarditis.
Subacute IE on a prolapsing mitral valve after dental work is most likely viridans streptococci from the mouth; benzylpenicillin-based treatment.
Rheumatic fever: eradicate group A strep with penicillin/amoxicillin; with penicillin anaphylaxis use a macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin).
IE in people who inject drugs is usually tricuspid (murmur louder on inspiration) and embolises to the lungs as septic pulmonary emboli.
Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK organism, often beta-lactamase-producing: switch to ceftriaxone for 4 weeks (6 for prosthetic valves).
Line-associated healthcare IE is most often S. aureus; remove the line, take cultures and give vancomycin until MRSA is excluded.
Sterile vegetations on both sides of the mitral leaflets are Libman–Sacks endocarditis of SLE (malar rash, non-erosive arthritis), especially with antiphospholipid antibodies.
IE after a urological procedure with a non-haemolytic, PYR-positive Gram-positive coccus is Enterococcus faecalis: amoxicillin plus ceftriaxone or gentamicin ~6 weeks.
Migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules and erythema marginatum meet Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent strep infection: a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B) titre.
A prolonged PR is a Jones (rheumatic fever) criterion, not a Duke criterion; in IE new conduction block may signal an aortic root abscess.

why: Key aligned with ESC/AHA (oral amoxicillin 2 g for prosthetic valve); explanation shortened

set.explanation: A prosthetic valve is highest risk: ESC/AHA advise single-dose oral amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before extraction. NICE advises against routine prophylaxis.
Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) IE is strongly linked to colorectal neoplasia, so isolating it should prompt colonoscopy.
Late prosthetic valve IE (> 1 year) resembles native IE; an acute illness after a furuncle points to S. aureus, which usually needs rifampicin and early surgery.
New hypertension work-up: U&E/eGFR, urine ACR and dipstick, HbA1c, lipids, ECG and fundoscopy. CT aortography is only for a specific clue.
ESH/ESC grades: 1 = 140–159/90–99, 2 = 160–179/100–109, 3 = ≥ 180/≥ 110 mmHg; 165/105 is grade 2. Confirm with ABPM/HBPM.
First-line: ACEi/ARB, dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic. Beta-blockers are used only for compelling indications (angina, MI, HFrEF, AF).
Addison's disease causes salt loss and hypotension. Conn's, acromegaly and 11β/17α-hydroxylase CAH cause hypertension.
A creatinine rise < 30% (eGFR fall < 25%) with K⁺ < 6 after an ACE inhibitor is expected; continue the drug and monitor.
Severe hypertension with papilloedema (acute organ damage) is a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension): admit for controlled IV treatment.
Hypertensive emergency needs a titratable IV drug (labetalol, nicardipine or nitroprusside); lower MAP by ≤ 20–25% over the first hours.
Systemic hypertension makes the aortic valve close forcefully, giving a loud A2. Aortic regurgitation softens A2.
Renal disease (parenchymal and renovascular) is the commonest secondary cause; primary aldosteronism is the commonest endocrine cause.
Apparent resistant hypertension is most often non-adherence (pseudo-resistance); exclude it, white-coat effect and NSAIDs before seeking secondary causes.
Systolic BP rises throughout life; diastolic plateaus or falls after 50–60 as arteries stiffen, hence isolated systolic hypertension in the elderly.
Heart disease (CHD, LVH, heart failure) is the commonest cause of death in hypertension; stroke is most tightly linked to BP level.
Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis despite an ACE inhibitor suggests primary aldosteronism (Conn's); check aldosterone:renin ratio.
Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone:renin ratio (correct K⁺ first); confirm by suppression test, then adrenal CT and venous sampling.
Malignant hypertension with encephalopathy and AKI: IV labetalol infusion, lowering MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour.
Albuminuria reflects generalised endothelial dysfunction and predicts CV events years ahead; hence urine ACR in the hypertension work-up.
Early renal artery stenosis raises renin (renin-dependent hypertension); a significant stenosis increases peak Doppler velocity.
Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, gout and hyperglycaemia. Ankle swelling is from dihydropyridine CCBs, not ACE inhibitors.
Grade 3 hypertension with LVH and grade 2 retinopathy but no acute features: start oral treatment now and review within days.
In type 2 diabetes NICE starts an ACE inhibitor at any age (ARB if Black or ACEi-intolerant); add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic next.
Hypertensive urgency (no acute organ damage) is lowered gradually with oral drugs; rapid ED reduction risks stroke and ischaemia.
About 90–95% of hypertension is primary (essential) with no single cause; secondary causes make up only 5–10%.
Keith–Wagener: 1 narrowing/silver wiring, 2 AV nipping, 3 flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, 4 papilloedema.
Hypertensive emergency with asthma: avoid labetalol; use a nitroprusside (or nicardipine) infusion, lowering MAP ≤ 25% in the first hour.
Before calling hypertension resistant, exclude non-adherence (pill count, drug levels) and confirm with ABPM; then seek secondary causes.
In diabetes with confirmed hypertension, start an ACE inhibitor alongside lifestyle advice (reduces albuminuria and nephropathy).
Daytime ABPM 138/85 is above the < 135/85 target on maximum ACEi: step 2 adds a CCB or thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide).
Gestational hypertension is new BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria; proteinuria makes it pre-eclampsia. Labetalol is first line.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant (vitamin K epoxide reductase; factors II, VII, IX, X). Aspirin, clopidogrel and dipyridamole are antiplatelets.
Digoxin is renally excreted, so hepatic impairment matters little. Renal impairment, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and amiodarone/verapamil precipitate toxicity.
Clopidogrel is a prodrug (CYP2C19) that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Omeprazole may reduce its activation; prefer lansoprazole.
Loop diuretics block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, the most potent diuresis; they cause hypokalaemia and alkalosis.
Evidence-based beta-blockers cut mortality by about a third in chronic HFrEF (start low when euvolaemic). They are harmful in acute LVF and cardiogenic shock.
AF rate control without heart failure: a beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB first (target < 110/min). Her CHA2DS2-VASc is 3, so anticoagulate too.
Oral anticoagulants cut AF stroke by ~two-thirds; apixaban beat warfarin with less bleeding (ARISTOTLE). Aspirin is not recommended.
Dipyridamole inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase and adenosine reuptake (raises cAMP). Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block P2Y12.
Mortality benefit in HFrEF is proven for bisoprolol, carvedilol and metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF); short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior.
GTN is mainly a venodilator: its benefit is preload (not afterload) reduction. Avoid in hypotension, RV infarction and after PDE-5 inhibitors.
NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins, causing salt retention that blunts ACEi; with a diuretic they form the 'triple whammy' for AKI.
ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10–15% (bradykinin accumulation), often weeks after starting; switch to an ARB.
Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that also blocks adenosine reuptake; MR dipyridamole + aspirin is used after TIA/stroke if clopidogrel is not tolerated.
Tirofiban (like eptifibatide, abciximab) blocks platelet GP IIb/IIIa, the final common pathway of aggregation; now mainly bail-out during PCI.
Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and risking rhabdomyolysis; withhold the statin during the course.
Exertional syncope in a young person suggests structural disease (HCM, AS, anomalous coronaries); echocardiography is the key test.
BLS is support of airway, breathing and circulation without equipment: call for help, CPR 30:2 and early AED. Drugs belong to ALS.
PEA is non-shockable: CPR, adrenaline 1 mg ASAP then every 3–5 min, and treat the 4 Hs and 4 Ts (e.g. hypoxia, hypothermia).
Atrial myxoma (75% left atrial, from the septum) can obstruct the mitral valve, embolise and cause fever/high ESR (IL-6); excise surgically.
The commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults is myxoma, a pedunculated LA mass on the septum; metastases are commoner overall.
In China-like populations, as CVD peaks, stroke mortality exceeds coronary mortality (high hypertension and salt intake).
The RA lies ~5 cm below the sternal angle, so venous pulsation above the clavicle when sitting upright means a raised JVP.
Pulse amplification makes systolic pressure higher and diastolic lower in distal arteries (leg SBP > arm, basis of the ABPI).
Normal conduction: SA node → atria → AV node → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles (endocardium to epicardium).
The P wave is atrial depolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the PR segment/QRS. T = ventricular repolarisation.
Normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°, so −20° is normal; −30° to −90° is left axis deviation.
Sinus rhythm with normal axis, intervals, R-wave progression and no ST shift or tall T waves: a normal ECG.
SA node cells depolarise spontaneously in phase 4 (funny current) faster than any other tissue, so they reach threshold first and dominate.
Multifocal/sinus tachycardia driven by pain, dehydration and hypoxia after a hip fracture: treat the cause (analgesia, IV fluids, oxygen).
Missed dialysis with a sine-wave ECG is pre-terminal hyperkalaemia: IV calcium, insulin–glucose and salbutamol, then urgent dialysis.
A denervated transplanted heart lacks vagal tone, so it runs at its intrinsic rate (~90–110/min) and responds only to circulating catecholamines.
Late after transplant, breathlessness without angina suggests cardiac allograft vasculopathy (denervated heart); diagnose by angiography.
Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is the commonest cause of secondary lymphoedema worldwide; cancer treatment in high-income countries.
Lymphoedema is protein-rich fluid, so diuretics do not help. Use decongestive therapy, compression, skin care and exercise.
PEA from massive haemorrhage will not reverse without volume: give blood products rapidly via the major haemorrhage protocol during CPR.
Sharp localised pain reproduced by palpation with normal ECG and CXR is musculoskeletal (costochondritis); no further tests, reassure and analgesia.
HFrEF on ACEi, beta-blocker and MRA: add an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), which cuts CV death and admissions with or without diabetes.
EF ≤ 30% > 40 days after MI: a primary-prevention ICD reduces mortality (MADIT-II). CRT needs LBBB with QRS ≥ 150 ms.
A resting rate of ~90/min in a well heart-transplant recipient is expected (denervation); reassure.
A donor heart tolerates only about 4 h of cold ischaemia, so it must be allocated within a limited radius of the donor.
In transplant-ineligible stage D heart failure, a durable LVAD (destination therapy) improves survival; inotropes do not.
CHD affects ~1% of births and ~90% of neonates now survive, so adults with CHD now outnumber children.
A flap that opens intermittently between atria is a PFO (~25% of adults), allowing paradoxical embolism; no treatment if incidental.
A small restrictive VSD with Qp:Qs < 1.5 and normal pulmonary pressures needs no closure; review periodically and maintain dental hygiene.
A coronary sinus saturation of 91% (normally ~30–40%) means arterial blood is entering it: a coronary AV fistula, causing a continuous murmur and steal.
Bicuspid aortic valve carries an aortopathy, so measure the aortic root/ascending aorta on every echo; repair at 55 mm (50 mm with risk factors).
Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RV hypertrophy. Tricuspid atresia is a separate cyanotic lesion.
Calcific AS of a trileaflet valve at 78 shares atherosclerotic risk factors: age, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, lipids, CKD.
Untreated severe AS: average survival ~5 years after angina, 3 after syncope and 2 after heart failure; any symptom means valve replacement.
Cardiogenic shock from critical AS: balloon aortic valvuloplasty temporarily relieves obstruction as a bridge to AVR/TAVI (restenosis within months).
Low-flow low-gradient AS with poor EF: dobutamine stress echo separates true severe AS (gradient rises, area stays ≤ 1 cm²) from pseudo-severe and shows contractile reserve.
In chronic severe AR diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens; LV end-diastolic volume, stroke volume and afterload all increase.
Acute severe AR: nitroprusside (± dobutamine) increases forward flow as a bridge to surgery. IABP is contraindicated; beta-blockers lengthen diastole.
Rheumatic heart disease is by far the commonest cause of mitral stenosis/LV inflow obstruction worldwide; annular calcification in the elderly.
In MS left atrial pressure rises to drive flow across the valve; LV end-diastolic pressure is normal or low and output falls.
Anything raising heart rate or output raises LA pressure in MS. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) lengthen diastole and lower LA pressure.
In MS, LA pressure falls with diuretics, valvotomy, cardioversion or rate control. Pacing at 90/min shortens diastole and raises it.
MVA 1.7 cm² is moderate MS; asymptomatic with exercise PASP < 60 mmHg, so review and serial echo every 1–2 years.
In secondary (functional) MR surgery does not improve survival, but transcatheter edge-to-edge repair reduced mortality in selected patients (COAPT).
Diastolic gradients RA > RVEDP and wedge > LVEDP mean tricuspid and mitral stenosis; no systolic gradients exclude pulmonary and aortic stenosis.
Functional TR from pulmonary hypertension is treated by diuretics, salt restriction and pulmonary vasodilator therapy; valve surgery is high-risk.
Doming pulmonary valve with peak gradient > ~64 mmHg is congenital pulmonary stenosis: percutaneous balloon valvotomy.
New severe MR gives the LV a low-pressure outlet, so EF rises while forward flow and the aortic gradient fall.
AF with moderate–severe rheumatic MS needs warfarin (INR 2–3) regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc; rivaroxaban was inferior (INVICTUS).
Peripartum cardiomyopathy risk factors: older age, multiparity, twins, pre-eclampsia/hypertension, African ancestry. Primiparity is not one.
A wheelchair-bound young man with scoliosis and DCM has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin); tall R in V1–V2 is typical.
Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant missense mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, TTN, LMNA); offer cascade screening.
TSH is part of routine tests in new heart failure, as hypo- and hyperthyroidism are reversible causes.
Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis has a good outcome if supported (inotropes, ECMO/VAD); LV function often recovers fully.
Giant cell myocarditis (with autoimmune disease) progresses rapidly with heart block and VT; immunosuppression helps but many need urgent transplant.
Anthracycline cardiotoxicity rises with cumulative dose (> 400–450 mg/m²), chest radiotherapy, heart disease, age extremes and trastuzumab.
Viral pericarditis (rub, diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, normal troponin): high-dose aspirin or NSAID with PPI plus colchicine.
In tamponade inspiration increases RV filling (tricuspid inflow) while LV filling and SBP fall (pulsus paradoxus).
Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal change or Q waves. ST elevation in V2 occurs in both, so it does not help.
Post-radiotherapy constriction (knock, dip-and-plateau) is treated definitively by pericardiectomy; diuretics give only temporary relief.
A pedunculated LA mass at the fossa ovalis with fever, arthralgia and TIA is myxoma: surgical excision without delay.
Melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer are commonest by number.
Commotio cordis: a precordial blow on the T-wave upslope triggers VF in a normal heart; immediate CPR and defibrillation save life.
Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in type 2 diabetes (2–4× risk, often silent ischaemia).
High-output heart failure in a heavy drinker that responds rapidly is wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency; give thiamine before glucose.
Hypothyroidism lowers heart rate, stroke volume and output, raises SVR and prolongs (not shortens) the QT.
Atherogenesis begins with LDL retention in the intima; oxidation, endothelial activation, monocyte recruitment and foam cells follow.
Arteries remodel outward, so a plaque does not narrow the lumen until it exceeds ~40% of the area within the internal elastic lamina (Glagov).
Statin benefit groups: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L, diabetes aged 40–75, 10-year risk ≥ 7.5%. Raised hs-CRP alone is not one.
HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors, niacin, fibrates) did not cut events; weight loss and exercise improve HDL and overall risk.
Myocardial oxygen demand depends on heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload); rhythm itself is not a primary determinant.
The heart already extracts ~70–75% of oxygen at rest, so extra demand is met by arteriolar dilatation and increased coronary flow.
Ischaemia shifts to anaerobic glycolysis: lactate and H⁺ accumulate (pH falls), ATP depletes, calcium rises and potassium leaks out.
Angina radiates to arms, neck, jaw, epigastrium and back; radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericarditis.
Peaked T waves with flat P waves are hyperkalaemia: give IV calcium gluconate first, then insulin–glucose and salbutamol.
Long QT from ST-segment lengthening the day after thyroidectomy suggests hypocalcaemia (parathyroid injury): measure ionised calcium.
S4 is atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it falls just after the P wave; S1 coincides with QRS. No S4 in AF.
Cardiogenic shock after MI: urgent PCI, with noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor (SOAP II), ± dobutamine. Routine IABP is not recommended.
Morphine is not recommended in acute heart failure, especially in shock (hypotension, respiratory depression, worse outcomes).
Acute MR (papillary rupture) into a small non-compliant LA gives a high wedge pressure with giant v waves. A saturation step-up in the RV suggests VSD.
Most sudden cardiac deaths occur in people without known heart disease or with EF > 35%; CAD underlies ~80% of adult cases.

1.explanation: Raised JVP with giant v waves, pulsatile liver and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge (louder on inspiration) is tricuspid regurgitation.

2.explanation: Bilateral ankle oedema with normal JVP and investigations in a treated hypertensive is amlodipine oedema (arteriolar dilatation); it responds poorly to diuretics.

3.explanation: COPD with hypercapnia (flap), raised JVP and oedema is cor pulmonale: right heart failure from hypoxic pulmonary hypertension.

4.explanation: Raised JVP, pericardial knock (early S3), hepatomegaly and ascites out of proportion to oedema with a small pulse is constrictive pericarditis.

5.explanation: Rheumatic disease with an apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla, soft S1 and loud S3 is severe MR, with secondary right heart failure.

1.explanation: Fever, rigors and pleuritic pain with dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over one zone is lobar pneumonia; assess with CURB-65 and CXR.

2.explanation: Sudden pleuritic pain in a tall young smoker with reduced expansion, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

3.explanation: Swinging fever despite antibiotics with dullness and absent breath sounds at the base is empyema; aspirate (pH < 7.2, pus) and insert a chest drain.
